I just watched this new horror film last night, and it gave me nightmares for days! It was  so  scary, I couldn’t even sleep without checking under my bed. Oh no, really? I haven’t seen it yet, but I heard it’s supposed to be one of the most intense films of the year. I’ve been meaning to watch it, but I’m not sure I’m ready. I’ve got a weak stomach for horror. You should try it, though. It’s got this one scene where the protagonist is trapped in a house with no lights and all these noises coming from the walls. It’s  not  for the faint-hearted! Yeah, I can imagine that. I still get scared by old classics like  The Shining  or  Hereditary . You know, the ones with the slow build-up and the psychological twist. Oh, I love that kind of horror. It’s not just about jump scares; it’s about making you feel unsettled, right? I think that’s what makes a good scary film. You stay up thinking about it all night, like, “What if that thing is actually real?” I totally agree. I think the best horror films are the ones that linger in your mind. You start questioning everything – like, are you safe at home? Are there things in the dark that you can’t see? Exactly! That’s what I loved about the film I watched. There was this one part where the camera lingers on a shadow moving in the corner of the room, and you just  know  something’s wrong. It’s so subtle, but it really messes with you. I would’ve been scared out of my wits! I’m not a fan of being alone in the dark. I always have the lights on, and I keep a flashlight next to my bed just in case. I used to be like that too. But now, I think it’s just part of the experience. You know, when you’re watching a horror film, you’re kind of  inviting  the fear in. It’s like a game. Maybe, but I still can’t shake the feeling that some of these films are watching us back. I swear I’ve seen something in the mirror when I’m alone. Oh, you’re not the only one. I’ve had that feeling too.

Good evening, love. I just got back from sorting out the new iPad for the kids. They’ve been asking for it for ages, and I thought now would be the perfect time to get them one before the holidays. Aye, that’s a good idea. I remember when I was their age, I used to wait forever for the new models. But I reckon now, with all the gadgets, it’s just part of life. Do you think they’ll use it much for school? Oh, definitely. They’ve got online lessons and all that. But I also thought about buying some new furniture for the living room. The old sofa is getting a bit worn out, and I’d like to make the place more comfortable for everyone. Yeah, I could see that. We had the same problem with the old chair I used to sit in. It was a bit of a pain to get up from. Maybe we could look into a new set from the furniture store down the road. I remember they have some nice options. That’s a good point. I was going to check the catalog tonight, but I thought I might ask you for your opinion. You’ve got a good eye for quality, you know. Speaking of which, have you seen the new Airbnb listings in the area? My cousin is thinking of renting out her place for the summer. I have, actually. Some of them are quite reasonable. I reckon it’s a good way to make some extra cash, especially with the way things are these days. But I wouldn’t mind staying at a place like that myself. It’s a nice break from the old house. I agree. I’ve been thinking about booking a trip somewhere. Maybe the coast? I’d love to take the kids to see the sea again. It’s been a while since we’ve had a proper holiday. That sounds like a plan. Just make sure you don’t get too caught up in all the gadgets and forget to enjoy the simple things. Like a nice pizza, for example. Ha! You’re right. I’ve been ordering pizza online too much lately. I think it’s time we go out and get a real one. Maybe even try that new Italian place the kids mentioned. Sounds perfect. Let’s make it a family night out.

Alright, I’ve just finished this book about the Highlands, and I’m still reeling. It’s like it’s taking me back to when I was a kid, running through the hills with my cousin. You remember that place? The one with those ancient stones and the moorland that stretched on forever. Oh yeah, I remember that well. I reckon it’s not just the book that’s making you nostalgic—it’s the way the author describes the air, the smell of heather, the way the sun sets over the glens. It’s like you’re there, isn’t it? Absolutely. I couldn’t help but think about that trip we took a few years back, the one where we got lost for hours and ended up in a village that didn’t even appear on the map. We ended up staying the night in a cottage with a roof that leaked, but it was one of the best nights of my life. Oh, you and your sense of adventure! I remember how you insisted we take the back road instead of the main one, and then we got stuck in a field with a flock of sheep staring at us like we were intruders. I still laugh about that today. And it was brilliant! We had the best cup of tea in that village, and the owner, an old man with a beard like a mountain, told us stories about the area like it was yesterday. It made me realize how much of the Highlands is still untouched, how much history and culture is hidden in those hills. It definitely does. I’ve been thinking about a trip back to the Highlands myself. I’ve got this idea to take a road trip, about five days, covering some of the remote areas. Maybe even take the Jacobite steam train. Have you ever been on that? Only once, and I’ll never forget it. The way the train moves through the landscape—it’s like you’re floating through time. You can see the hills, the glens, the lochs, all in one breath. It’s magical. I’d love to experience that. Maybe we can plan it together. I’ve got a book on the rail routes, and I’m pretty sure the service is still running. It would be a great way to combine travel with exploring the culture and history of the region.

I just got an email from the architecture firm I applied to. They want to schedule an interview, but it's in London and I’m not sure if I can make it. Oh, that's exciting! You've worked so hard on that application. Are you worried about the timing? A bit, honestly. I was supposed to start at my current job next week, and I don’t want to leave them hanging. But this opportunity is really important to me. I understand. You’ve always been so passionate about architecture. But if it’s a big chance, you should go for it. I mean, you’ve got the skills and the experience. Thanks, Mum. I appreciate that. But what if I can’t make the interview? I don’t want to look unprofessional. You don’t have to worry about that. Just let them know you’re working on a project and maybe propose a different time. I’m sure they’ll be flexible, especially if you’re a good candidate. Yeah, but I don’t want to give them the impression I’m not committed. What if they don’t like the idea of rescheduling? They’ll understand. Employers are used to people having responsibilities. Besides, you’ve got a great track record. You were the best in your postgrad class. That’s true. I just don’t want to make a mistake. I’ve been so focused on my current role, and now this new opportunity is coming up. It feels overwhelming. It’s natural to feel that way. But you’ve always been so capable. Let me help you draft an email to the firm. I’m sure you’ll do great. That would be amazing. I’d feel better if I had someone to review it. Of course. I’ll set up some time later today. Just remember, you’re not alone in this. I believe in you. Thanks, Mum. You always know how to make me feel confident. I’ll take your advice and go for it. That’s my girl. You’ve got this. I can’t wait to hear the good news. I’ll let you know as soon as I do. I promise. And if you need anything else, just let me know. I’m here for you. I know. Thank you, Mum. I couldn’t do this without you. Always.

I've been thinking a lot lately about how times have changed, haven't they? When I was young, we had proper jobs and a sense of purpose. Now, it's all about sitting around waiting for the government to do something. Not that I'm complaining, but things feel a bit... uncertain. I couldn't agree more, old chap. I remember when we had the benefit of the doubt, and people were more willing to work. These days, it's like we're all just waiting to be rescued. I keep telling my wife, "If only we could go back to the days when we had to earn our keep!" Oh, don't get me started. I still remember working with children and having a purpose, even if it wasn't a nine-to-five job. But I do miss the days when we had more security. Nowadays, even if you're retired, it's like you're still waiting for the next crisis to hit. Speaking of which, what’s the deal with housing prices? They've gone up so much that it's almost impossible for anyone to afford a home these days. I mean, we used to have decent houses with gardens, now it's all about apartments and commute times. I’ve got a friend who's stuck in a flat in London, and it's costing him more than his mortgage used to be in Norwich. Oh, I know that feeling. I've been trying to find a place to live for years, and the prices just keep going up. I think it's a complete scandal. The government should be helping people, not making it harder for them to get a foot in the door. I hear you both. I've been trying to find a place to downsize, but everything's so expensive. I keep thinking, "What's the point of living in a place that barely pays for itself?" I mean, I still have the house in Harrow, but I don’t use it much anymore. It's more of a burden than a benefit. Yeah, I can see that. I think the whole system has gone off the rails. I’ve seen so many people struggling, and I just don't know how to help them. I mean, we're all retired, but we can't even afford to go out to dinner without feeling guilty.

I've been thinking about the space conversion again. That old warehouse on the east side—do you think we could really turn it into a co-working hub? It's got a lot of potential, especially with the café and event space we're planning. It's a great idea, but I'm not sure if we're ready yet. The fire escape needs more work, and the storage isn't up to standard. Plus, we still haven't got the insurance sorted. Have you spoken to the insurance broker about that? Not yet, but I was going to ask you today. I think we need to make sure we cover all bases. Also, I've been looking at the supply chain for the new furniture. It's going to cost a bit, but it's worth it for the brand image. Absolutely, but we need to be careful with the budget. I was thinking we could do a phased rollout, starting with the main office area. Maybe get some quotes from local suppliers first. Do you have any ideas on how to market the new space? I was thinking about a launch event—something that combines a networking mixer with a short exhibition showcasing local artists. It would attract the right kind of attention and help us build a community feel. That sounds good. But we need to make sure we have enough people on hand for the event. I'll talk to the staff about rotating shifts and making sure there’s holiday cover. Oh, and I’ve been meaning to ask—what’s the update on the tenants? We’ve had a few new inquiries, especially from start-ups and small businesses. I think the conversion will make a big difference in attracting them. We've also been talking with the local council about partnerships. They’re interested in supporting green initiatives, so maybe we can highlight that. That’s a great angle. Let’s make sure to include that in our marketing. I’ve also been thinking about the maintenance schedule. The bird problem in the rooftop garden is getting worse. Do you think we should install some netting or something? Yes, and maybe arrange for regular clean-ups. It’s not just a matter of aesthetics—birds can cause damage. I'll set up a meeting with the maintenance team to discuss it. Perfect. And if we can get some funding from the council for the bird netting, that would be ideal.

I can't believe how good this roast is. I mean, I’ve had a few in my time, but this is next level. Maybe it’s the Welsh lamb? Oh, you’re not wrong. This lamb is from a local farm, just outside Hereford. My cousin runs it. He’s been telling me about how they treat the sheep like royalty. They even play soft music in the pens. I think that's more of a myth, but if it makes you enjoy the meal more, then why not? I’ve got to say, the way you season the lamb here is different from the way I grew up in Bristol. I always used to cook it with garlic and rosemary, but this is more of a traditional Welsh thing, isn’t it? I think it's the herbs they use. I’ve been trying to find out where they get them from. I saw a sign earlier that said ‘Welsh Mountain Herbs’ or something like that. Maybe it’s the local blend that gives it that extra kick. That’s probably it. I remember my grandmother using a mix of thyme, sage, and a bit of oregano. She said it made the lamb taste like the hills of Wales. I tried to replicate it when I was cooking for my kids – it didn’t quite work, but I think it was the lack of experience. I did a similar thing with my own family. I used to cook it with a bit of cider, just to give it a slightly sweet note. It was a family tradition. I can still remember the smell wafting through the house and my mum being all, “That’s the best lamb you’ve ever had, love.” Oh, I know that one! My mum used to cook it with some sort of local honey and a splash of vinegar. It was a bit strange, but the kids loved it. I think it’s that combination of sweet and savoury that really ties it all together. Speaking of which, I was wondering if we could try making a Welsh lamb recipe as a family. It’s something we can all take part in. Maybe we can all contribute our own twists. That way, we get to share our heritage through food. That sounds fantastic. I know my cousin would love to be part of it.

So, do you ever miss the city? I mean, I do. I know it's busy, but there's something about the noise and the pace that keeps me going. I mean, sure, sometimes I feel like I need a break, but I can't imagine living anywhere else. Honestly, I do miss it too, but not in the way you do. I miss the people, the culture. I mean, I've been working in the countryside for a few years now, and it's just not the same. You can't just step out and be surrounded by the same energy. Yeah, I get that. I mean, I've been to the south a couple of times for work and it's nice, but I always end up missing the rhythm of the city. I think I'd go crazy if I moved away. I mean, the food alone—there's just nothing like the street food in the city. That’s true. I remember once we went to Leeds and there was this little stall selling these weird pies that looked like they had everything in them—cheese, meat, maybe even some weird sauce. I ate it and thought, "I’ve never had anything like that before." It was insane. Oh, I remember that. You said it was like a meatball but with more flavor, and way more than you should eat in one go. Still, I love that kind of thing. I think it's one of the things that makes the city so unique. The people are always so passionate about what they do, whether it's food, music, or just talking. Exactly. It’s like everyone has a story. I mean, even the most random person on the street has a life you wouldn’t believe. I think that’s part of what makes it so interesting. You never know what you’re going to hear next. That’s what I love about it. It’s like you’re always learning something new. I mean, I used to think I knew all about the North, but I’ve learned so much just by being there. Like, I didn’t know there were so many different dialects and traditions. Yeah, and it's not just about the dialects. It's the way people live, the way they celebrate, the way they raise their kids. There's a real sense of community that I don’t think you get in the south.

I just got a call from the hospital. My dad’s having another scan. It’s been a real rollercoaster, hasn’t it? I’m trying not to get too worked up, but it’s hard when you’re used to being the one who’s always in control. I can only imagine. My mum had a similar situation last year. She was diagnosed with something serious, and it was so hard watching her struggle. I think I’ve been trying to be strong for her, but honestly, it’s exhausting. Yeah, I know what you mean. It’s like you’re walking on eggshells all the time, worried about saying the wrong thing or not being there enough. Have you talked to your mum about the funeral arrangements yet? Not really. I know we need to do something soon, but I’ve been avoiding the conversation. It feels too final, you know? I guess I’m just not ready to think about it. How are you coping with your dad’s situation? Honestly, I’m not sure. I’m trying to be brave, but there are moments when I just break down. I’ve been talking to my sister about it, and she’s been a huge support. She’s even suggested we all take a walk together, just to get our heads straight. That sounds nice. I think I need to do something like that. It’s just so hard to deal with all of this alone. I’ve also been thinking about my own health lately. I’ve been trying to eat better and not overindulge. I know it’s not the same as what you’re going through, but it’s hard to stay positive when your own body feels like it’s betraying you. I can relate. I’ve been trying to be more mindful of what I eat, especially since I’m stressed. I’ve even started cooking more at home. It’s strange, but sometimes cooking helps me feel more in control. Though I have to admit, it’s a lot easier said than done. I’m trying, honestly. I’ve even been cutting back on the snacks. It’s not like I’m a complete foodie, but I do love a good cup of tea. I think I’m just trying to find a balance. It’s one of the few things I can do for myself, really.

So, do you two remember when we went skiing in the Alps last winter? It was the first time I’d ever tried it, and I nearly fell off the slope after my first run. I think I might have been more excited than ready! Yeah, you were so nervous you kept checking your phone for directions every five seconds. I swear, you didn’t even know how to stop properly until you hit a tree. It was hilarious. I remember that. You two were so out of your comfort zones. I was just enjoying the view from the lodge, watching you both try to master the slopes. I actually ended up getting a better tan than you two combined. Yeah, you were like a tourist in a movie. I mean, I got so sick of you two talking about the "best" wine you’d ever had in the world, even though you’d only tried a couple of bottles. I just wanted to go skiing! Oh come on, that’s not fair! We were just sharing our experiences. Besides, I did end up getting a nice bottle of red from that village—my favorite so far. It paired perfectly with the fondue we had later. Yeah, but you also got so distracted by it that you missed the whole point of the trip. You know, skiing, not wine tasting. I barely had time to finish my first run before you were already asking about the wine labels. You two are like the stereotypical wine and food lovers. I still think you two should have gone to a wine festival instead of a ski resort. You’d have been much happier. Honestly, I think I’d rather be at a car show than either of those. I mean, I just watched my dad’s old BMW 320i for the first time in years. It’s a classic, and it smells like he never cleaned the inside. It’s like a time capsule. A time capsule? That’s a bit dramatic. But I’ll admit, there’s something nostalgic about driving an old car. I just finished up a client project last week, and I had to print out all these documents. It was so tedious, but it reminded me of the good old days. That sounds exhausting. I had my own work experience last summer, and it was nothing like that.

I just found this old photo of us in Japan, remember? We were in Kyoto, and it was the first time we ever took a proper trip together. It feels like a lifetime ago. Oh, I remember! You were so excited about the temples and the food. I think you even tried to eat all the sushi in one sitting. It was ridiculous. Yeah, I was on a mission. I swore I would master the art of sushi before we left. And I thought I had, too. But then we got to the market and you insisted we try the raw octopus. I don’t even know how I walked back to the hotel. You were still alive, though. And you didn’t throw up. That’s a win in my book. Anyway, I still have the photo you took of us in front of the Kinkaku-ji Temple. It’s one of my favorites. You looked so happy. I know, right? It’s such a perfect moment. I wonder if we’ll ever get to go back. I’ve been thinking about Japan a lot lately—especially the badgers. You remember that one we saw near Nara? How could I forget? We were watching them from a distance, and then one got too close. You tried to take a photo, but it was so fast, you missed it. You were so upset. I laughed so hard I almost cried. I still get annoyed when I think about it. I was ready to take the perfect shot. And then they just disappeared. I swear they were mocking us. You’re being dramatic. They were just doing what badgers do. You know, about as dramatic as a group of squirrels arguing over acorns. I suppose you’re right. But that doesn’t make it any less frustrating. Still, I’ll take the photo we took of the badgers. It’s better than nothing. Absolutely. And besides, it was one of the reasons we ended up going to Japan in the first place. You wanted to see them, and I wanted to see the temples. We made the best of it. That’s the thing about travel, isn’t it? You never know what you’ll find. Even badgers can turn into a memory worth keeping. Exactly. And I’d say we’ve got a lot more memories to make. Maybe we should plan another trip soon.

Alright, so I just got back from Ireland, and I have to say, it was wild. I mean, I got to see the Cliffs of Moher, and I even tried a pint of Guinness. But honestly, the best part was when I went skinny-dipping in a lake near the mountains. It was freezing, but it felt like I was one with nature or something. Oh wow, really? I mean, I’ve only ever tried that in a pool, and it was just a bit of a shock. But you’d think the Irish would be more into it, considering the weather. Wait, did you go near the west coast or the north? I think the west coast is more like that. I’ve been there once, and it’s so picturesque. But I wouldn’t go skinny-dipping in the sea, I’d be too cold. Although, I did hear a story about a guy who did it in a lake and ended up with a severe case of hypothermia. He looked like a ghost for a week. That’s terrifying. I mean, I do like the idea of going skinny-dipping, but I’m not quite there yet. I think I need more of a reason. Maybe if it was during a zombie apocalypse, I’d be more open to it. You know, hiding in the water, and zombies can’t swim… Exactly! It’s like, if the world’s ending, then why not jump in the lake, huh? Although, I don’t think zombies would be the first thing on my mind. I’d be more concerned with finding food and shelter. Hey, you know what I’ve been thinking about? This new photo app I found. It’s called SnapRecipe, and it lets you take a picture of a dish and it tells you how to make it. I tried it with a lasagna, and it said something like ‘stir the sauce’ and ‘add more cheese.’ It was wild. That’s not wild, that’s just confusing. I tried using it once with a Jewish recipe from Claudia Roden. It said ‘soak the chickpeas for 24 hours’ and then took a picture of the water and said something like ‘victory!’ Oh man, that’s classic. I mean, Claudia Roden is amazing, but the app probably doesn’t understand the nuance of Jewish cuisine. Though, honestly, I’d rather take a picture of a kugel and get a wrong recipe than try to make it from scratch.

So, do you remember that time we were at Alton Towers and I tried to ride the Dragon? I was so scared, I thought I was going to die, but I did it anyway. Oh yeah, that was one of the worst experiences of my life. I was with you, and I was just as scared as you were. I didn’t even want to get on the ride in the first place. I know, I know, but you said you wanted to try something new. And then you ended up screaming the whole time. I was just trying to be brave, like you! But I guess I wasn’t brave enough. Still, I’ve never been back to a theme park since. I can’t believe you didn’t go back. I still go to them every chance I get. But then again, I’ve got a soft spot for all the rides. Maybe it’s because I’m a PhD student and I don’t have the energy to deal with roller coasters. I prefer to be in my lab, surrounded by books and computer screens. You’re not as brave as you think. You once tried to beat me in a computer game, and you lost. That was a fluke! I was just lucky. And besides, I’m not the only one who’s bad at games. You know, I was the one who taught you how to play  Call of Duty  in the first place. Oh, come on, that was a long time ago. Also, I didn’t just learn from you—I got better at it  because  of you. I know, but you still beat me every time. I think you just have a natural talent for video games. Well, I do have more time to practice, don’t I? Plus, I play every night. Yeah, but I’m working on my thesis, and I don’t have time for games. I’m too busy worrying about border security. What? Why are you worried about border security? I’ve been reading a lot about it lately. I think it’s important for the country. But I’m also worried about how it affects people who are just trying to live their lives. I get what you mean. It’s all so complicated. But I think we should focus on things that bring us joy, like peanuts, films, and theme parks.

I can't believe I've just managed to row a straight line for five minutes without capsizing! I thought I’d be drowning in the river by now. You're doing brilliantly! It’s not easy, especially if you’re used to the calm waters of a lake. I remember my first time in a kayak—literally, I capsized within ten seconds and ended up with a full face of water. I’ve never looked at a lake the same since. Oh, I’d love to try kayaking one day. But I keep thinking about the weather. It’s been so wet lately, and I don’t want to get soaked and end up with a cold. I’ve been thinking about buying some proper waterproof gear. That’s a smart idea. Yo, man, it's been ages! You've been in Japan for ages, right? How's that going? Yeah, man, it's been like six months. I'm still getting used to the pace of life there. I just got a new phone, and I'm so used to it now. It's like having a personal assistant in my pocket. But I still can't get the damn Facebook app to work properly. So, how was your holiday in Belgium, Mum? I heard you had a bit of a time with the sat nav, and I’m not even sure I’m allowed to use mine in the UK anymore. I just finished making the pasta sauce. It’s a bit too spicy for my taste, but I think it’ll work with the lamb. Maybe we can tone it down a bit when we serve it? You always do that, you know. Just like the old days, when we used to gather around the fire and talk for hours.

I've always been fascinated by Australia. I remember reading a book once about the people there—their way of life, the landscapes. But I've never actually gone. I suppose I'm one of those people who's always thought about it but never made the move. I can relate. I’ve always wanted to visit too, but with the state of the economy and everything, it's hard to plan a trip. I remember hearing about the business men in Australia—they dress so differently, you know. It's not like the UK. You’d think they'd be more formal, but no, they wear those casual suits with the ties that look like they've been tied in a hurry. Oh, I've heard that too. I think it's part of the culture. In Sheffield, we have our own dialect, you know, and it's quite different from the south. It's all about the way you pronounce words. I remember when I was teaching in Bristol, a student from the south said I sounded like a Yorkshireman, which I didn’t even think I was! Oh, I know what you mean. I used to teach in Bristol too, and the difference in accents is quite striking. I always felt like I was in a different country just by walking into a classroom. But I suppose that's the beauty of England, the diversity of accents and dialects. Yeah, and don’t get me started on the Sheffield dialect. I went to a pub once in Sheffield and the conversation was so fast, I couldn’t follow a word. I thought I was in a game of charades! It's not as bad as you think. It's more about the rhythm than the actual words. Once you get used to it, it's quite charming. I once had a student from Queensland who said the Sheffield accent reminded him of his grandmother's voice. He was from Brisbane, so he found it quite warm and familiar. That's funny. I've heard similar things. People often assume that all Australians are the same, but I think the diversity there is just as rich as in the UK. I’ve read that Queensland has its own distinct culture and dialect, just like Yorkshire does here. I think that’s true. I’ve met a few Aussies who have lived in the UK and they all have different stories about how they adapted.

I just checked my Instagram again, and I'm so tired of seeing the same people posting about their yoga retreats and avocado toast. It's like everyone's trying to be  too  woke. I know, right? I feel like I'm constantly scrolling through content that makes me feel guilty for not being vegan or not having a podcast. It's exhausting. Yeah, and I mean, I love podcasts. I actually listen to a few every week. My favorite is the one about British history. It's so informative, and it's just the right length. Oh, I’ve heard of that. I used to teach part-time, but then I stopped after I got laid off. It’s been a few years now. I just can’t find anything stable. I can’t imagine being unemployed for so long. I mean, I’ve always been in a lower managerial role, but I’ve never been without work. It’s odd how people can just vanish from the job market. It’s weird, isn’t it? I mean, I was educated, I had a graduate degree, and I was even semi-retired. But somehow, I ended up unemployed. It’s like the system just forgot about me. That’s really sad. I can’t even imagine that. But hey, at least you’re still here, and you’re not stuck in a dead-end job. I think I’d rather be unemployed than be in the wrong job. True. But I do miss the structure of having a routine. I used to have a lot of friends, but I’ve lost touch with most of them. It’s hard to stay in touch when you’re not working. I get that. I’ve been trying to stay in touch with my friends, even though I’m busy. We all have lunches, or we meet up for coffee. Some of us even do online meetups. That’s a good idea. I need to start doing that. I think I’ll try to meet up with some of the old friends. Maybe even join an online podcast or something. Yeah, that sounds like a good plan.

I can't believe it's already Saturday. I've been looking forward to the weekend for ages, especially with Pippy and Blue Peter coming over. I was trying to tie them yesterday and ended up with a big knot. It looked like a spider web! I saw that! You look like a giant spider. But it's okay, we all make mistakes. Some people believe it, but I think it's just a myth. I bet ANON’s circus is going to be amazing. I can't wait to see the elephants and the acrobats. I can't wait either. It's going to be a great day. Just make sure you both bring your pocket money for the rides and snacks.

Right, so I was just talking to my cousin about this, and she’s been like, “Oh my God, have you ever thought about sex?” I mean, sure, but I’m like, “Wait, we’re 19, what’s the big deal?” Yeah, I mean, it’s not like we’re suddenly going to be like, “Oh no, we’re adults now and we have to deal with all this stuff.” It’s just… weird, you know? Like, I keep thinking about it, but then I’m like, “Wait, am I even ready for that?” Yeah, I feel that. I mean, I know it’s natural, but it’s so much more complicated than I thought. I mean, I’ve seen these ads about erectile dysfunction and it’s making me really anxious. Like, what if I can’t even do it? What if I’m not… you know? Oh wow, so you’re already overthinking it? I mean, it’s not like we’re in a relationship yet, right? We’re just like, you know, friends who like to hang out and watch Netflix. But still, I keep thinking about it. Like, what if we actually… you know? Oh come on, you don’t even have a boyfriend! You’re still in the middle of your degree, for God’s sake. Who are you even talking about? I know, but you know what? I think I’d be okay with it. Like, I’m not scared of it, but I do worry about the actual mechanics. Like, what if I’m not… you know… I’ve seen this documentary about it, and it’s like, “Oh, it’s normal to have anxiety, but if it happens too much, you should see a doctor.” Yeah, I think I’ve read something like that too. You know, it’s not like we’re over 40 or anything. But still, it’s a little scary. I mean, I’ve heard about people who can’t even get it up, and I’m like, “Wait, I’m not even supposed to be… you know…” Okay, okay, let’s not get too dramatic. It’s just sex. I mean, we’re both students, we’re both 19, we’re both healthy. We’ll figure it out when the time comes. Yeah, I guess. But I do wonder, like, what if we’re like, “Oh no, we’re not even good at it?”

I can't believe we've got all this stuff to cook for Saturday’s treat day. We're going to need a proper plan, or we'll end up eating more than we should. I've been thinking about the Slimming World Healthy Extra options – they have those 0 calorie syrups and artificial flavours. I mean, is it really healthy if it's got no calories? Oh come on, you’ve got to be careful what you wish for. I’ve tried the 0 calorie syrup, and it’s basically just water with a hint of artificial stuff. It doesn’t even taste like real syrup. But the thing is, sometimes the healthy options are still high in syns. I mean, cauliflower cheese with a roast is a great meal, but I’ve seen some recipes that make it look like a mini Lasagna. I’m even thinking about using Siri to set a reminder for our exercise targets.

I've been thinking a lot about our holiday plans. I really want to go somewhere with good food and a bit of culture, maybe somewhere in Europe. Oh, that sounds nice, but I’m not sure I’d be able to handle the heat. I get too hot too easily. What about somewhere like Tuscany? The weather is milder, and the food is amazing. I’ve always wanted to drive through the countryside, maybe stop at some vineyards and see the old castles. That could be a great idea. I have, but I’m still not sure where to start. I keep getting distracted by other things, like politics and tattoos. It would be something quiet, maybe reading in the garden, having a nice cup of tea, and just being with you.

I've been thinking about the birthdays this weekend. I know you mentioned wanting to have a small gathering, but I’d like to make sure we have enough food and drinks for everyone. That’s a good point. I was going to suggest the same thing—maybe a potluck? It’s less stressful and gives everyone a chance to contribute something they enjoy. I like that idea. Though I’ve been meaning to ask, have you managed to get the postcard I sent you from Scotland? I think it’s one of those old ones with the hills and the castle. Oh, yes! I’ve had it on my desk for a while. I’ve been meaning to frame it. It’s a nice reminder of the trip we took last summer. The views were incredible, especially near the loch. I remember. But I have to say, I don’t think I’d want to live in a country that’s not part of the UK. There’s a certain familiarity and sense of tradition that comes with being British. I agree. But at the same time, I can see the appeal of independence for some people. They might feel more in control of their own destiny. And if we’re getting the postcard framed, I can take it to the shop this week. I’d like to have it ready for the party. Perfect. I just saw a news story about the Syrian refugees coming into the UK. I was thinking, maybe we could do something to help. You know, like drawing a chair for them? A chair? Like, a real chair? No, not a real chair. A drawing. We’re doing an art project at school where we draw chairs for people who need them. It’s supposed to be a way to show kindness and empathy. Cool! Can I draw a chair too? Of course you can. But first, we need to think about what kind of chair we should draw. Do you know what kind of chair a refugee might need? Maybe a folding chair? Like the ones you see at school assemblies? That’s a good idea. Folding chairs are versatile and easy to carry. But let’s also think about comfort. A refugee might need a chair that feels safe and familiar. What if we draw a chair with a cushion? That’s a wonderful idea. Comfort is important. I think the chair should represent a place of rest and safety. Maybe we can also add a little table and a cup of tea, like a cozy corner in a home. Oh, like a little room in the chair? Exactly, like a tiny home. It’s a creative way to show that even in difficult times, there’s a place to belong. Can I draw a chair with a picture of a cat on it? That’s a great idea! Some people like to have a pet or a familiar object with them. It adds a personal touch. Maybe we can all draw different chairs and then display them in the living room. I can draw a chair with a book on it. I like reading. Perfect. We can have a little gallery for the chairs. It will remind us that even small gestures can make a big difference. And it’s something we can all do together. I’ll draw a chair with my toy dinosaur. That’s fantastic. We’ll have a little collection of chairs that show the world from different perspectives. It’s a beautiful way to learn about empathy and kindness. Can we do this next week? Absolutely. Let’s make a plan. We can start with the drawing and then maybe even write a short message or story to go with each chair. It will be a meaningful project for everyone.

I just got a message from Lucy saying she’s pregnant again. She’s got two already, and now she’s expecting her third. I’m so excited for her, but I can’t help feeling a bit jealous. I just had the most ridiculous dream last night. I was walking through a forest and suddenly, a policeman came up to me and said, “You’re not allowed to walk here without a permit.” I asked him, “What’s the law about that?” And he said, “It’s called the ‘Witchwood Regulation’—if you’re not registered, you can’t enter.” I woke up in a sweat, thinking, “What if it’s real?” Oh, you’re not the first to have that. My cousin once told me he had a dream where a woman in a red coat came up to him and said, “You’ve been cursed by a ghost from the 17th century.” He woke up and thought, “That’s just a dream,” but he’s still scared of red coats now. So, do you think shmeat is the future or just another gimmick? I mean, I’m vegetarian, but I’m not sure I’m ready to eat lab-grown meat yet. Honestly, I think it’s a step in the right direction. So, do you remember that time we tried to visit France last summer? I was so excited, thinking it would be like the movies, but honestly, I got more lost than I ever have in Aylesbury! So, do you ever notice how people’s accents can tell you so much about where they’re from? So, do you know what’s the biggest language challenge when you travel? I was in Spain last year, and I got lost because I couldn’t understand the locals when they spoke quickly. I can't believe we've got to this point. That coffee machine we bought last year is still going, and yet we're still arguing about whether it's worth keeping or not. So, do you remember that band we used to listen to in uni? The one with the weird lyrics and the really loud guitar riffs? I still have that cassette tape somewhere. Oh yeah! Hey, do you think this book would be good for the kids? I mean, it’s about family trees and stories, right? Yeah, it’s pretty cute. I think it could work. So, do you remember when we were kids and we used to play that alphabet game where you had to say a word starting with each letter? It was so much fun. I've been thinking a lot about the St. Michael's Hall project. The grant application is due in two weeks, and I’m not sure we're on solid ground with the bid. I've seen too many projects where the funding body pulls out because they don't see a clear plan. I know what you mean. I had a similar issue with the old mill in Dorton. We were told the funds would be allocated for preservation, but when they saw the budget details, they said it was too risky. You need to present the workable business plan like it's a story, not just a list of numbers. Exactly! And I've been trying to get the local council on board. They've been pretty supportive, but I think they're still waiting for the final draft of the business plan from the Heritage Foundation. It's like they're holding their breath for approval. That's a common problem, isn't it? I mean, they all want to be part of the solution, but they don't want to be seen as the ones who made the decision. It's a bit of a balancing act. You have to be clear about who's responsible for what, and how the funds will be used. I agree. I've been working on a revised version of the plan, focusing more on the community benefits. We're planning to set up a heritage centre that will serve as both a museum and a venue for events. It could generate income and bring more people into the area. That sounds solid. I think that's a good angle. You should definitely highlight the community aspect in your bid. Funding bodies love to see projects that benefit the local area beyond just the building itself. I did something similar with the Dorton bridge project, and it paid off. I'll make sure to include that. By the way, have you heard anything from the council about the funding for the local museum? I was wondering if they might be interested in contributing. Not yet, but I'll check with them this week. I can also mention your project to them as a potential partnership. They’ve been talking about expanding their own heritage initiatives. That would be great. Let's set up a meeting with them next week. I'll bring the updated plan and see what they think.

I just got back from a trip to the Lake District, and I have to say, it was absolutely stunning. I got to visit some of the places I read about in my linguistics research—like Keswick and Penrith. It’s incredible how the landscape influences local dialects. That sounds amazing! I’ve always wanted to go there. I’ve been thinking about doing some fieldwork on dialects in the North of England. I mean, I’ve got my PhD on regional variations, and I’ve been trying to find some under-researched areas. Didn’t you hear about the new dialect preservation project? Oh, I did! I think it’s funded by the AHRC. It’s about capturing the spoken language in rural areas before it disappears. I was really impressed by how much variation there was in pronunciation and vocabulary. I mean, even between Sunderland and Newcastle, there’s a noticeable difference. Exactly. I’ve been thinking about doing some interviews in Birmingham, but I’m not sure how much variation there is. I mean, the Midlands have a distinct accent, but I’m not sure if it’s as consistent as the North. Have you noticed anything in the Lake District? Definitely. One of the things that struck me was how the dialects there have been influenced by the Industrial Revolution. There’s a lot of old words and phrases that have survived. I even heard someone use the word “brolly” for an umbrella—something I’ve only heard in the North before. That’s interesting. I was thinking about how urbanization affects dialects. In cities, people tend to speak more standard English, especially in professional settings. But when they’re at home or with family, they slip back into their local dialect. Do you think that’s changing with the internet and social media? I think it’s evolving. There’s more exposure to different dialects now, especially with people from different regions interacting more. But I still think there’s a strong sense of identity tied to local speech. It’s part of what makes a place unique. I agree. Language is such a vital part of culture. I keep thinking about the research I’m doing and how it connects to people’s personal histories. It’s not just about words—it’s about how people express their identity. Exactly. And I think that’s why I love my job.

I just can’t get over the film we saw last night. It was so gripping, wasn’t it? That scene where the protagonist confronted the antagonist—unreal, but I felt like I was there. I've been thinking a lot about the war lately. You know, how it changed everything for us. I was just a kid when it started, but I remember my dad talking about how people were so worried about the future. Yes, the war had a huge impact on everyone. I was in Harrow, and there was a lot of rationing and fear. My mum used to tell me how she had to queue up for bread every morning, and it was never enough. It really shaped how we grew up. It was a difficult time, but also a time of great resilience. My family had a small business, and we had to adapt quickly. We had to make do with what we had and trust in the community. It was tough, but we got through it. I remember the war from a different angle. As a child, I was lucky enough to be in a school that had a strong sense of duty and community. We were taught to be proud of our country, and it really influenced how we saw the world. That's true, but I think the war also changed the way people looked at the world. You know, it made people more aware of the dangers and the importance of peace. It made us all more cautious, in a way. Definitely. I think it also made people more distrustful of authority, especially the police. I remember hearing stories about how the police were sometimes too strict, and that made people feel uneasy. I think the police played a big role in maintaining order during the war. But I also remember how they were very strict with civilians, especially during the blackout periods. It was a time when people had to be very careful about how they behaved. Yes, the police had a lot of power back then. I think it was part of the reason people were so wary of them. It made the whole idea of law and order feel a bit oppressive. I think it's strange how the war still affects how people think today. I mean, even now, when I talk to my grandchildren about history, they're always curious about how things were back then. I agree. I think it's important for people to remember the past, especially the parts that taught us about resilience and the cost of conflict.

I’ll see if they can speed things up. And if not, we’ll have to come up with a plan. I just hope we can find something that feels like home again. Yeah, same here. I just got the list of guests for the birthday meal, and I think we need to discuss the table plan. It’s going to be quite a few people, so seating arrangements will be important. Yeah, I know. We’ve got the extended family, a couple of friends, and even a few colleagues. I was thinking of putting the grandparents on one side and the younger generation on the other. It seems like a good way to keep things organized. That makes sense. It will help with conversation flow. We need to make sure the seating doesn’t put anyone too far from the main dishes or the cake. We’ve got a few guests who are into the Great British Bake Off, so maybe we can get some themed candles? That’s a fantastic idea. I’ve seen some really creative ones online. I swear, I’m gonna take out my wisdom teeth when I get back to uni. They’ve been hurting like mad ever since I got back from France. It’s like they’re trying to tell me something, but I don’t know what. Oh, you’re not the only one. My cousin had hers done last year, and it was a nightmare. I hope you don’t end up with an infection. I heard that if you don’t take care of it, it can spread really fast. I think I’m just gonna deal with it until I get back to uni. But I’m telling you, if I have to go through it, I’m gonna make sure I take all the painkillers the doctor gives me. I mean, I’m gonna be in Doncaster again, so I’m not moving. But it’s nice to hear you’re getting settled. I’m still trying to figure out if I’m gonna rent a place or stay with my parents. They’re not too happy about me living on my own. My parents are really into that whole “you should be with family” thing. I think they’re worried about me. But I’m almost 21, so I think I’m allowed to make my own decisions.

I've been thinking about doing some random acts of kindness this month. It's the perfect time, especially with Chinese New Year coming up. Maybe we could all do something meaningful together? That sounds lovely! I love the idea of helping others, especially around the holidays. What kind of things could we do? I don’t know, maybe we could donate some food to the local shelter? I heard they’re always in need. That’s a great idea. I was also thinking of making lactose-free cakes and cookies for the community center. I’ve been experimenting with recipes and they’re turning out really well. Oh, that sounds delicious! I’d love to help you with that. I can bring some ingredients from home. I can help too! I’m pretty good at mixing and baking. Maybe we can make a big batch for the center and also give some out to neighbors? That would be wonderful. And don’t forget, Chinese New Year is a time to give and receive. Maybe we could also help out with some decorations or write cards for the elderly? I think that’s a brilliant idea. I’ve been wanting to do something like that for a while. What do you think, Dad? I think it’s a great plan. I love giving gifts, and making things for others makes me feel happy. Perfect! I was also thinking about doing some small acts of kindness in the neighborhood. Like leaving notes in people’s mailboxes or helping someone with their groceries. That’s so sweet. I can help with that too. I love making people smile. I can help with the notes. Maybe we can make a little list of kind things we can do and share them with everyone. That sounds like a perfect way to organize our ideas. And with Chinese New Year coming up, it’s a great opportunity to celebrate giving. I’m really looking forward to it. Me too! I hope we can all do something meaningful this month. It’ll be such a nice way to start the new year. Yeah! Let’s do it. I can’t wait to help out with everything. I think it’ll make us all feel really good. Exactly. Let’s make this a month of kindness and joy. I think we’ll have a great time together. Alright, let’s get started!

I just had the weirdest dream last night. I was in a giant chessboard made of seagulls. It was so weird, but also kind of beautiful. Seagulls? You’re still dreaming about that seagull incident from the beach? You were so scared when it swooped down and almost knocked your hat off. Yeah, I know! It was so close. I still have a little scar on my forehead from where it brushed past. I was reading Alice in Wonderland that day, and it was like the book came alive. You always did have a vivid imagination. Remember when you were little and you dressed up as Alice and tried to jump into the pool? My husband still laughs about that. I was  so  serious about it. I even brought a little red dress and a teacup made out of a plastic bottle. You know, the kind of thing you’d find at a DIY store. Oh, I remember. You were so focused on the costume that you forgot to wear a life jacket. My husband had to pull you out of the water. You were quite a dramatic child. Well, I’ve grown up a bit since then. I’m into music now. I’m learning to play the guitar, and I even joined the school band. It’s amazing how something as simple as music can change your life. That’s wonderful. You’ve always had such a passion for music. I remember when you first told me about your dream of performing on a stage. You were so nervous, but you had such a pure voice. Yeah, I still do. I even got a chance to perform at a local theatre last month. It was so much fun. I was singing a song from the musical  Hamilton . You’re doing great, sweetheart. I just wish I could sit in the audience and see you shine. Speaking of which, did you get a present for your birthday? I did! It was a new guitar. I’m so excited to start learning more songs. That’s perfect. I’ll be there for every practice session. You know, I think you’re going to be really something special. Just like the character in  Alice in Wonderland . You always say the sweetest things, Mom. I love you. I love you too, sweetheart. Now go on, practice your guitar. I’ll make some tea and we can talk more later.

I just had a call from the solar panel group last night, and they’re really grateful for the advice we gave them. It’s amazing how much local knowledge can influence the outcome, even when you're up against a powerful energy company. That's true, isn't it? We've seen it time and time again. But I still think the issue with wind turbines is different. They're not just about aesthetics; it's about the actual location and how it impacts the local wildlife and landscape. It's a bit of a double-edged sword, really. You can't deny the need for renewable energy, but you can't ignore the environmental cost either. Exactly. And I'm still amazed how the local council seems to be on the side of the big energy companies. It feels like there's a real lack of transparency. But I suppose that's the politics of it all. You've got the planners, the developers, the politicians—everyone has their own interest. And don't forget the financial side of things, too. I've heard that the government gives way more money to subsidize solar and wind than it does for research into better storage solutions. It's a bit like putting the cart before the horse. You can't have renewable energy without the proper infrastructure to store it. Yeah, that's a valid point. I mean, it's all well and good having a lot of wind turbines, but if you can't store the energy when the wind isn't blowing, what's the point? I think there's a need for more innovation in battery technology and other forms of energy storage. I agree. I've been reading up on some new developments in solid-state batteries and hydrogen storage. I think those could be game-changers. But it's all very technical, and I'm not sure how much local groups can do without outside support. That's where the funding comes in. If the government is willing to invest more in research, maybe we could see some real breakthroughs. But I don't think they're going to change their approach anytime soon. We're stuck in a loop of subsidies and short-term gains. I think it's also about public awareness. People need to understand the bigger picture. The Scottish referendum in two weeks is a good chance to get that message across.

I've been thinking, love, about when you're going to get your licence. You've been asking about it for ages now. I suppose it's about time you started learning. Yeah, Dad, I know. I've been saving up for the lessons and the test. But I was also thinking about the car insurance. I don't want to get stuck with something too expensive. Oh, I remember when I first got my licence. I had to save up a fortune just to get the car. But now, with the way insurance works, it's a bit different. Yeah, but it's still a big expense. I heard that if you're a young driver, the insurance rates are pretty steep. You might want to get a used car, maybe something older, to keep the costs down. That’s a good point. I was thinking about buying a second-hand car. I’ve been looking at some online listings. I found a few cars that look pretty decent for the price. Well, I’d advise you to drive carefully. I remember when I first started, I was a bit nervous. I think the best thing is to take your time and be safe. You don’t want to be in an accident right away. Exactly. And remember, it's not just about the car. It's about being responsible. You're not just driving for yourself, you're driving for the family. We all need to be safe on the road. I know, Dad. That's why I'm taking the lessons seriously. I want to make sure I'm ready. I also want to make sure I'm not putting anyone in danger. That's what counts. And you're not alone in this. I'm here to help. Maybe I can give you a ride to the driving school if you need it. That’s a good idea. And maybe we can all go on a holiday together at the end of the month. You know, to celebrate when you get your licence. That would be great. I’ve been thinking of a holiday to Cornwall. It’s a nice place to relax and enjoy the sea. I’d love to take the whole family. Cornwall sounds lovely. I've always wanted to go there. I think it's a great idea. Just make sure you don't go too far away before you're fully qualified.

I just got a new phone, Dad. It's got this fancy app for betting on horse racing. I thought it might be useful, but honestly, I’m more confused than ever. I've been trying to figure out how to cash out, and I keep getting these weird notifications about mobile data. Oh, I remember when I used to place bets back in the day. It was all about the paper tickets and the horse racing form. You’d have to mark your bets with a pencil and then wait for the results to come in. It was like a game of patience, not just chance. Yeah, but I guess it's easier now, right? All you need is a phone and a bit of luck. My friend Lucy said she started betting on Facebook. She says it's more social, like you can talk to other people and share tips. But I don’t know if I trust that. Hmm, I’ve heard of that. But I’d be wary. People can be very misleading on social media, especially when it comes to betting. You never know who’s really giving you the real info and who’s just trying to get your money. True. I tried to sign up for the app, but I kept getting these pop-up ads about food banks. It's like they're trying to tell me I'm not in a good place financially. I feel like I’m getting more notifications than actual useful stuff. Oh, you’re not the only one. I’ve had the same problem. I’m not sure why they keep pushing those ads. I mean, I’m retired, but I still have my pride. I don’t want to be seen as someone who needs help. But I do know that food banks are there for people in need. I guess I’m lucky. I still have a job and a place to live. But I can see how tricky it can be for someone like you, Dad. I heard about some people who have disabilities and don’t get the benefits they deserve. It’s a real shame. Yeah, I know. It’s sad to see how the system can fail people. I’ve heard stories from my old colleagues, and it’s not just about money. It’s about feeling left behind and not having the support you need.

So, do you remember that time we tried to act out a Shakespeare play in front of our mates? I think it was  Romeo and Juliet , but we completely butchered it. Oh, I remember! You said “To be or not to be” like you were trying to solve a murder, and I was pretending to stab you with a pencil. It was  so  dramatic. Yeah, I think I got more attention for my dramatics than the actual play. But honestly, it was one of those moments where you just want to win the admiration of the group. You know, like,  I’m the Shakespearean genius here.  I’d say you were more like the one who accidentally started a war with a pencil. But hey, that’s what makes the story funny, right? Exactly. But I was thinking – what about the whole ‘skill learning’ thing? Like, I’ve been trying to get better at golf, and I keep telling myself I’m going to ‘win’ the next game. But I just end up taking more swings than the pro. You’re not winning, you’re  losing with flair . And honestly, you’ve got better form than half the people I’ve seen at the club. You’re just not aiming for the right hole. Yeah, I know. But I think it’s the same with everything. You try to win, and then you just end up with a nickname. Like, I got called ‘The Golf Whisperer’ because I once hit the ball so far it landed in someone’s garden. Oh, and then you got called ‘The Accidental Pro’ for a week. I still remember your face when the ball went over the fence. You looked like you’d just committed a crime. I told you I was just trying to be dramatic. Anyway, what about your surname? I always thought it was like a nickname. You know, like ‘Speck’ or something? No, it’s just ‘Smith’. My dad’s a bit of a traditionalist. But I’ve always thought it’s kind of cool. It’s like,  I am the common man, and I will not be named after a random fruit.  Fair enough. But I’m still trying to figure out why my surname is ‘Watson’. I mean, I can’t even pronounce it properly without sounding like I’m from a different planet. Well, you’re from Exeter, so I guess it’s just one of those things.

Right, so, I’ve been trying to get my work routine sorted. I’m co-ordinating a conference next month and I’m going mental trying to find a venue that’s affordable but still decent. Did you guys hear about that new event space in York? Yeah, I did. I reckon it’s got all the bells and whistles but I doubt it’s got the budget for anything but a basic setup. You’re not gonna be able to do much with it, mate. You might as well stick with the old place in Leeds. I can see what you mean. I’ve been thinking about moving out of my flat in Lewisham, too. Rent’s gone up again and I’m not even sure if I can afford the deposit on a new place. I’m thinking of moving in with my cousin in Milton Keynes, but I’m not sure if that’s a good idea. Oh, I know what you mean. I’ve been trying to save up for a deposit, but with the cost of living, it’s like trying to climb a mountain. I’ve been eating more takeaway and less fresh stuff. It’s not healthy, but it’s cheaper. Yeah, I’ve been doing the same. My mum says I’m a disgrace, but I reckon if I can’t afford a proper meal, I don’t see the point in eating properly. Though I did try to go vegan for a week—horrific. I had a salad with a sauce that tasted like a shoe. That’s not even close to my most disastrous meal. I once tried a health bar that was supposed to be high in protein. It tasted like cardboard and I felt like I’d been hit by a truck. I haven’t touched that stuff since. I can imagine. I tried that too. You know, I was thinking about going to a weekend festival next month. You two wanna come? It’s in Manchester and I know a few people who can get us discounted tickets. Manchester? That’s a long way from Cambridge. I’ve got to work Saturday, but I could do a Sunday. If it’s not too far, maybe. What’s the vibe like? It’s supposed to be really vibrant. There’s live music and food stalls. I’d love to go.

I've been meaning to call you all for ages, but with the weather being so damp, it's been hard to get out. How's the garden doing down your way? I’ve been having a look at the old hedges and thought maybe we could have a chat about the new painting programme on TV. Oh, I’ve been watching that one too. It's fascinating, really. Though I don’t know how much of it I can take in these days. Still, it’s good to keep the mind active. And the garden? Well, the roses are coming back, but the neighbours have been up to no good again with that fencing. That’s always the way, isn’t it? They like to encroach on everyone’s space. I've got an owl box up by the old oak tree, though. I thought it might help with the little creatures that come in the evenings. And the bamboo we planted last year—well, it’s growing like mad. I remember the day we planted that bamboo. It’s a shame we didn’t get it properly rooted. I was thinking, maybe we should have gone with some native shrubs instead. But it’s too late now, I suppose. How are you feeling, love? You’ve been looking a bit peaked lately. Oh, I’m fine, thank you. Just the usual. I’ve been trying to eat better, though. We’ve been talking about the TV licence again—can you believe the government’s trying to make us pay for it again? I don’t know how much longer I can justify it. It is a bit of a shame. But you know, I’ve been cooking more, trying to eat well. I’ve been experimenting with different vegetables. Have you tried the new cosmos seeds I planted? They’re coming up nicely, and the bees are loving them. I’ve seen them, yes. They look like little fireworks. I’ve been thinking about the eclipse too. I remember the last one was quite something. I’ve been telling the kids about the beginnings of space and the black holes—how they pull everything in, even light. That’s what I’ve been reading about. I’ve been trying to get my head around it all. It’s so strange, really. But it’s also pretty mind-blowing. You know, I’ve been wondering if we could go on a tour of the garden one of these days.

So, do you know where the best fish and chips in Sunderland is? I was just thinking, since we’re heading back, maybe we could grab something proper before heading home. Fish and chips? You’re talking about the traditional stuff, aren’t you? I mean, I know it’s a bit of a cliché, but I’ve heard the place by the river is good. Is that near the old train station? Yeah, I think so. I remember my nan used to take me there when I was a kid. She said the chips were so crispy, they could stand up on their own. But I guess it’s been a while since I’ve had the real thing. Oh, I get it. You’ve probably been eating takeaway too much lately. I know I have. You know, I was in Manchester last week and there’s this place called The Gherkin that’s supposed to be amazing. But I just found out they actually have a real fish and chip shop there too. The Gherkin? That’s the building, right? The one with the glass and the shape like a cucumber. I mean, that’s not a fish and chip shop. That’s a fancy building. But I guess it’s got a restaurant in it. Maybe you’re right, maybe it’s worth checking out. Exactly. It’s all about the experience now. But I still think the real thing is better. You know, the old-school kind of thing. I mean, when I was in Harpenden, there was this little place run by a guy with a beard, and he’d shout at customers and it was all part of the charm. Harpenden? I’ve heard of it. I think it’s near Hemel Hempstead. I’ve never been there, but I’ve heard it’s got a lot of Victorian houses. You know, like the kind of place you’d see in films. I’d love to see one of those. Oh, I know. I’ve driven past them a few times. They’re everywhere in Hertfordshire. But I also want to take you to a cathedral one of these days. I mean, not just for the architecture, but because it’s a place where people can go and really think. That sounds nice. I’d love to see a real cathedral. I mean, I know the ones in the North are pretty big.

Good morning, Mavis. I couldn’t sleep last night. The birds were singing like a symphony. I think it’s the skylarks again. You know how they sound, like they’re singing from the sky? Oh, I know. They’re the ones that sound like they’re singing from the top of the world. I’ve been trying to identify them for weeks now. I even got one of those birdsong apps. It’s like a puzzle. You always did love your puzzles. Remember when we used to try and guess which bird was singing at what time? I swear, the blackbirds were always the worst. They sound the same no matter what time of day it is. And the robins, of course. They’re always so loud, like they’re arguing with the world. I still remember the time I thought I heard one singing in the garden at 2 a.m. I thought I was dreaming. Turned out it was just the wind. Well, I’ve been trying to feed the birds a bit more lately. I got this special seed mix, and they love it. I even got a bird feeder from the local market. It’s made of wood, just like the old days. That’s lovely. I’ve been thinking about doing the same. I’ve had this old feeder in the attic for years. I just never got round to installing it. But I’ve been reading up on bird feeding. They say you shouldn’t feed them fat and seeds all the time – it’s bad for their health. Oh, I know. I’m watching what I feed them now. Maybe I should start giving them some mealworms. I heard they’re good for their feathers. Speaking of birds, did you hear about the dentist? My neighbor had a nosebleed during her appointment. She said it felt like the whole room was shaking. What? Is that true? I’ve heard of people getting nosebleeds from the dentist, but I didn’t think it was that common. Are you sure it wasn’t just a coincidence? I don’t know. But I’ve been told that sometimes when you get older, you just can’t take the pressure. I suppose it’s all part of growing up, isn’t it? Oh, I know. It’s all part of the package. You just have to make the most of it while you can.

I can't believe it's been five years since we last saw each other! It feels like it's been decades. How have you been? Oh, I’ve been good, thank you! I’ve actually been through a lot recently. I tried IVF again last year, and it was... challenging. I mean, I wanted to be a mum so badly, and it just didn't work out the first time. I had to go through the whole process all over again. That must have been so hard. I'm so sorry to hear that. I know how much you've wanted a family. Did you end up getting pregnant this time? No, unfortunately not. I decided to take a break and focus on my career for a bit. I've been working more hours lately, and I just felt like I needed to take a step back. It's been tough, but I’m trying to stay positive. That’s understandable. I remember when I was going through the same thing. I ended up becoming a single parent through adoption. It was a huge lifestyle change, but it's been worth it. I’ve never looked back. That’s incredible. I admire your strength. I’ve been thinking about starting a book about single parenthood and the challenges we face. It's something I want to share with others who might be going through similar situations. That sounds amazing. You have such a unique perspective. Have you thought about how social media plays into this? I mean, it's such a big part of our lives now. Oh, yes! I find it both helpful and overwhelming. There's so much support online, but it’s also easy to compare yourself to others. I’ve started using yoga to help me cope with stress. It’s been a real game-changer for me. That’s great to hear! I do yoga too. It’s like a little reset for my mind. I’ve also been thinking about changing my career. I’ve always wanted to write, so I’m working on a novel. It's such a big shift, but I feel ready for it. That’s so inspiring. I think you’ll be amazing at it. You’ve always had a way with words. I hope you get it published soon! Thank you! I’m really excited, but I know it'll take time.

I just had a cup of tea with my neighbour, a retired teacher from Birmingham. He's quite a character—always got a story or a comment about everything. Oh, I know him. He's the one who used to teach English, right? He says he's retired now, but he still gives lessons every now and then. I think he's got a real passion for language. Yes, he mentioned he used to teach in a school in the Midlands. I think he was quite strict, but respected. He said he's got a lot of students who are still in touch with him. That's typical of teachers. They always seem to have a connection with their students, even after they've retired. I remember my old school teacher telling me stories about the kids, even after they left. I think he's got a point. I was a language teacher too. It's strange how the bond between teacher and student can last for years. I still get messages from former students, especially on special days like teacher's day. It's a good thing, really. I used to think that once you left the classroom, it was all over. But I've found that many people still cherish the lessons they learned. Exactly. I was talking to my brother the other day about his own school days, and he said he still gets a lot of advice from his old teacher. It’s funny how that works. It’s kind of like someone who knows you best. They’ve seen you through the good and bad times. I think that’s why people keep in touch, even as they grow older. Definitely. I remember when I was about to leave university, my English teacher gave me some really good advice. It really helped me in my career. That’s the thing about education. It leaves a lasting impact, even after you’ve left the classroom. It’s like a foundation for life. I couldn't agree more. I think that’s why we need to keep learning, even after we’ve retired. It keeps our minds active and our spirits high. Well said. I’m thinking of starting a book club or something like that. Maybe with some of the old friends I still have from teaching days. That sounds like a great idea. It could be a way to stay connected and keep learning from each other.

Alright, lads, I’ve got a load of takeaway chicken tikka masala for us. Should be nice and spicy, and it’s from the same place as last week, so I know it’s not going to be a complete disaster. Oh, you picked the same place again? I thought you were going to try something new. It’s always good to mix it up. I know, I know, but I’ve been too busy with work. And honestly, I’d rather not risk it. We’ve had the same thing for weeks now, and it’s still good. You know what I mean? Yeah, I get it. I mean, I always go for the same curry place in Pembury. It’s got that rich, creamy sauce that just hits the spot. You can’t go wrong with that. I’m actually in the mood for something different. I was thinking of trying that new sushi place down by the river. They’ve got some really fresh fish, and the prices aren’t too bad. Sushi? You sure? I thought you were going to stick with the classics. You don’t want to end up with a lukewarm roll and a stomach ache, do you? He’s got a point. I remember last time I tried a new place, I ended up with a huge portion of raw fish and nowhere to put it. It was a mess. I’d love to try the sushi, but I’m still not sure. But I think I’m ready for something a bit more exciting. I’ve been meaning to try it for weeks. Well, if you’re up for it, I’m happy to go. But if you want to stick with the masala, I’m totally fine with that too. We can compromise. You know what? We could do both. We could have the chicken tikka for tonight and head to the sushi place tomorrow. That way, we get the best of both worlds. That sounds good to me. I’m always up for a bit of variety. Just don’t expect me to eat sushi every single day. I’ll need a break. Exactly. So, what time are we meeting?

Alright, so I just got back from this weekend trip to the coast. I know it's not exactly a big deal, but I thought I'd check out this new gym I heard about in Exeter. It's this super modern place with all these high-tech machines. You know, the kind that actually make you want to work out. Oh, really? I heard about that gym too. I think it's called Fitness Nexus? I tried to go once, but it was so packed I couldn't even get a spot on the treadmill. You’re the first person who’s actually made it. Yeah, I’ve heard of it too. I think it’s got the latest VR fitness stuff. I was like, “Wow, that sounds futuristic.” But I’m not sure I’d ever use it. I’m more of a push-up and yoga kind of person. I can't believe the Euros are already in full swing. It's like the whole country's been on a football high all weekend. I watched the England vs. Scotland game last night—what a thriller! Oh, look at this, Maeve. This is our grandson, Eoin. He’s just turned seven, and he’s already got this infectious laugh. We’ll take him to fun fairs, to the cinema, and maybe even to Iceland again.

I just made a really lovely stew. I think it’s going to be the best one I’ve made in ages. What do you think? It smells amazing! I can already tell it’s going to be a hit. I still remember the story, even though I’m almost 90 now. That’s a classic. I remember the snow globe and the magical world where everyone speaks different languages. It’s such a heartwarming story. And it’s one of those books that makes you feel like you’re part of the adventure.

I've been thinking, you know, about the old days. Back when we had proper jobs and real work. It feels like a lifetime ago now. I know, love. I sometimes wonder what it would be like to have that kind of routine. But you know, I’d rather be doing what I'm doing now, even if it's not much. At least it keeps me busy. Yeah, I suppose. I’m here for you, always. And I always will be.

Hey, how’s everyone doing? It’s been ages since we last caught up. I’ve been so busy with work, and I missed our chats. I know, I've been trying to get in touch too. I've been thinking a lot about the housing situation in Liverpool lately. It's gotten pretty tough, especially for people like me and my colleagues who are in the higher professional brackets. I just got a postcard from Nepal. You know, that mountainous place with all the beautiful temples and the tea houses. I thought we could go there next summer. I just got a message from the local library about their plans to close next month. It's such a shame. I mean, how are we supposed to get access to books and resources if they've got no place to go? I’ll start drafting the petition today. We can meet at the café tomorrow to run through it. I’ll bring some coffee, and you can bring your brain-training tips. Sounds perfect. Let’s make sure the library stays open.

I've been thinking a lot about the Jehovah's Witnesses lately. They've been knocking on our door more than once, and I've got to say, I’m more than a bit suspicious of their ways. I just finished transcribing those logs from the weekend. I couldn’t believe the variety of accents they had. It’s like a language festival in there! I know, it was quite a mix. I've been thinking a lot about buying a house these days. It’s a bit of a nightmare, isn’t it? You've got all these taxes now—council tax, stamp duty, and then there's the upkeep. I don’t know how people even afford it. Oh, don’t get me started. I remember when we were young, you just signed the contract and that was it. Now you’ve got to worry about energy bills, insurance, and then there's the mortgage. It's like you're paying for the house twice over. I can’t even imagine. He says he’s in a council house now because he can't afford a deposit. Yeah, I heard about that. My brother-in-law tried to buy a place five years ago, and he didn’t have the down payment. We used to have a pub there called The Red Lion. It’s been closed for ages now. I hear the new owner is going to convert it into a café, but I don’t know if that’ll go well. It's all about change, isn’t it?

My grandma once tried to make it, but her onions burnt. Classic. I remember my aunt trying to make it once too. She ended up with a little too much garlic. But you know, it's all part of the charm. I bet we’ll find some fresh produce and maybe even some local wines to go with our meal.

I've been thinking, lass, about that debt collector who called last week. I told ‘em I couldn’t pay and they said they’d be back next week. I don’t know how we’re going to manage it, Elsie. I’ve been out of work for ages. Oh, I know, Bob. I’ve had the same thing. I reckon it’s not easy for anyone these days with the economy the way it is. But we’ve got to be careful with our finances. I’ve started to track every penny I spend, even for the little things like seeds for the garden. You know, like those sunflowers I bought last week. That’s a good idea, Elsie. It’s easy to get carried away with little things. I’ve been doing the same, actually. You know, I even used the computer to track my expenses. It’s a bit of a hassle, but I think it helps.
